[EMERGING] Can AI keep track of facts that keep changing? 🧠

The Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) released StateBench, a test of "state tracking": following how information about people or objects changes across very long texts. It has four difficulty levels.

All four frontier models tested handled the easier levels well, but on the hardest, longest problems their accuracy fell to 13% or lower. Some alternative model designs trained on the task generalized almost perfectly on three of four levels.

Caveats: this is a preprint, not yet peer-reviewed, and scores changed a lot depending on how the same problem was framed.

[TODAY] AI keeps getting more efficient per task. So why is its power use climbing? ⚡

Think of LED bulbs: each one uses less electricity than the old kind, but if we keep switching on more of them, the total bill still goes up.

The International Energy Agency reports that electricity demand from data centers grew 17% in 2025, far faster than global demand (3%). It expects data center use to double by 2030, with AI-focused centers growing even faster. The IEA notes that power per AI task is falling rapidly, but more people use AI and energy-hungry uses such as AI agents are rising.

[IMAGINE] What if you rarely opened apps again, and your assistant used them for you? 📱

What's real: on November 3, 2026, Apple opened Siri AI to all developers through a Developer Preview. Apps can plug into the assistant, and "skills" can combine several actions into a single experience. It is a beta for developers before shipping to customers in a few months, and it's currently unavailable in the EU on iOS, iPadOS and watchOS.

What we imagine: you say one sentence and the assistant books, pays and reminds across several apps. The big open questions are trust, mistakes and who stays in control.

[EMERGING] Quantum bits are famously fragile. What if you could make one that almost never slips?

Quantinuum reports that on its 98-qubit Helios machine, it grouped up to 37 physical trapped-ion qubits into a single "logical" qubit protected by error correction. It reports a logical fidelity of 99.9995%, about five errors per million operations. Science News puts the error-suppression gain at about 10x per step up in code size.

Caveats: these are company results in a preprint, not yet peer-reviewed, for a single logical qubit. Science News notes useful machines would need roughly 50 to 100 of them.

Sources (link in bio):
Quantinuum press release, Oct 19, 2026
Science News, Oct 20, 2026, "megaquops" error correction

[TODAY] Someone could photocopy your locked diary today and simply wait for a master key to be invented. 🔐

That's "harvest now, decrypt later": attackers can capture encrypted data now and try to decrypt it once quantum computers are powerful enough. NIST's new guidance on moving to post-quantum cryptography (NISTIR 8547, October 2026) flags this risk. US federal policy sets 2035 as the primary target for the switch.

Why start now? NIST notes that past moves to new encryption standards took 10 to 20 years, and estimates of when quantum computers become a threat range from a few years to a few decades.

[IMAGINE] What if planes, ships and even phones found their way using Earth's magnetic "fingerprint" instead of satellites? 🧭

What's real: Earth's magnetic field varies from place to place, and quantum sensors can measure it precisely enough to match against a map. In a 2026 test reported by DefenseScoop, an Embraer 170 flew about 4 hours 23 minutes over the Pacific without GPS. The testers report accuracy 89% better than traditional backups. Separately, Q-CTRL reports up to 111x better positioning on a 700 km flight with Airbus (a company claim).

Caveat: these are trials, not certified airline systems.

Where would GPS-free navigation matter most? Tell us in the comments.

[TODAY] Solar farms are learning to save sunshine for later. ☀️🔋

According to the US Energy Information Administration, over 16% of the new utility-scale solar capacity added in the US in 2026 has a battery operating at the same site, up from 2% in 2017. Counting projects planned for the rest of the year, that could reach 19%, and developer plans for 2027 and 2028 point to more than 30%.

Caveat: future figures come from plans, which can change. Solar makes up about 13% of total US utility-scale generating capacity.

[TODAY] Power grids are built like highways for rush hour: big enough for the single busiest moment, even if it lasts only an hour.

That peak keeps climbing. The US Energy Information Administration reports that Texas's grid (ERCOT) hit a record 91.1 GW on July 22, 2026, 6.5% above its previous record. The PJM grid, serving the mid-Atlantic and parts of the Midwest, peaked at 162.6 GW on July 2.

The idea: if some flexible use, such as charging or cooling, moves outside the busiest hours, the peak gets flatter and the grid may need fewer new "lanes." It helps, but it can't replace all new capacity.

Sources (link in bio):
US EIA, Today in Energy, Oct 15, 2026, "PJM, ERCOT, and SWPP all set peak load records this summer"

[IMAGINE] What if we drilled for heat the way the oil industry drills for oil, almost anywhere? 🌋

What's real: Fervo Energy says its Cape Station in Utah, an enhanced geothermal plant, connected to the grid on September 24, 2026 and declared commercial operation on September 30. Its first unit produces 33 MW of net power. The company plans about 100 MW in its first phase and an additional 400 MW expected in 2028.

Caveats: these are company claims about a first-of-its-kind plant, and how well the approach works elsewhere depends on local geology.
